newsitem.title: CANADA: Poll shows strong opposition to anti-Cuba law.
newsitem.headline: Poll shows strong opposition to anti-Cuba law.

text.p: Most Canadians and almost half of Americans oppose a U.S. law that punishes firms doing business with Cuba, according to a poll released on Tuesday.
The poll, conducted by Canadian pollster Angus Reid, found almost eight in 10 Canadians and about 48 percent of Americans were against the Helms-Burton law.

Helms-Burton, signed into law by U.S. President Bill Clinton in February 1996, seeks to compel third countries to join U.S. efforts to isolate Cuba by penalizing companies and executives that do business with the Marxist island state.
The measure is the thorniest dispute between Canada and the United States, the world's largest two-way trading partnership. The European Union has also complained about the law.

The only Canadian company directly affected so far is Sherritt International Corp., whose executives have been barred from entering the United States because of the company's mining and agricultural activities in Cuba.

The telephone poll was conducted in March 1997 among a cross-section of 1,000 Canadian adults and 1,004 American adults. The results were 95 percent certain within plus or minus 3.1 percentage points.

Slightly more than half the Canadians polled said they strongly opposed the anti-Cuba law and 24 percent said they were moderately opposed to it, Angus Reid said. Only 13 percent favored the legislation.
Among Americans, 27 percent of the respondents said they moderately opposed Helms-Burton and 21 percent strongly opposed it. But almost as many -- 45 percent -- said they were in favor of the law.
